title: Does Practicing on an AI Actually Work?
author: Mike Kentz
summary: Mike Kentz surveys published research on LLM-based role-playing simulations—what he calls 'friction bots'—as learning tools across five domains: medical education, counseling, history, teacher preparation, and negotiation. He reviews a JMIR RCT in which AI-simulated patients outperformed traditional case-based training by over six points in internal-medicine knowledge scores; a Stanford/Georgia Tech CARE study isolating that AI-generated feedback (not AI practice alone) drives improvement in counseling microskills; Benjamin Breen's UC Santa Cruz medieval peasant simulation that generated historical empathy at scale; a TeacherGen@i virtual classroom for pre-service teachers; and Columbia's ACE negotiation coach, which outperformed both no-feedback and alternative-feedback conditions. The consistent finding across domains is that LLM simulations add learning value when combined with structured feedback, embedded in a larger instructional cycle, and not deployed as one-off engagement activities. Kentz openly acknowledges his commercial interest in this approach—he is building a platform—and invites readers to weight his synthesis accordingly. His core argument is that LLMs uniquely solve a scalability problem: role-play and rehearsal have long been known to be effective, but human-to-human simulation is resource-intensive and hard to access; AI-enabled friction bots extend that practice to contexts and populations that couldn't previously get reps. What the field still needs, he concludes, is the pedagogical infrastructure—the craft of designing virtual rooms and simulated conversations—to be codified across a wide range of educational contexts.
points: Across five domains (medicine, counseling, history, teacher training, negotiation), LLM-based role-playing simulations produced meaningful learning gains when paired with structured feedback and embedded in a larger instructional cycle—establishing friction bots as a scalable supplement to human simulation, not merely a novel engagement activity.

The CARE counseling study isolates the critical variable: practice-alone with an AI patient showed no improvement (and led to declining empathy), while practice-plus-AI-generated-feedback significantly improved client-centered microskills—suggesting that the feedback mechanism, not the simulation itself, is what drives learning.

Benjamin Breen's medieval peasant simulation at UC Santa Cruz demonstrates that LLMs can generate historical empathy at scale—students inhabited randomised peasant personas across 500 years of European history—but gains only emerged when simulations were integrated into a larger cycle of discussion, analysis, and reflection.

Columbia's ACE negotiation coaching system improved performance across both a no-feedback condition and an alternative-feedback condition, building on the insight that negotiation training is traditionally limited to resource-intensive seminars that most learners never access—a scalability problem AI simulation directly addresses.

The pedagogical infrastructure surrounding a simulation matters as much as the simulation itself: pre/post reflections, discussion, and portfolio artifacts that trace the arc of student learning converted AI role-play from an engagement activity into a genuine, evidenced learning intervention.
quotes: I’ve been writing for a while about academic role-playing exercises and conversational simulations that are designed to push back. I call them friction bots. When I talk to other educators about their value, especially professors, I often get the question, “Ok, but what does the research say?

The VSP students showed a theoretical score improvement roughly six and a half points higher than the control group (17.07 mean vs. 10.67). The authors concluded that the virtual experience reinforced foundational internal-medicine knowledge, enhanced clinical thinking ability, and improved capacity for independent work. They called the system feasible, practical, and cost-effective.

Furthermore, with respect to empathy, the practice-alone group declined over time and performed significantly worse than the feedback group. And, when researchers interviewed participants, the ones who received feedback adopted a client-centered listening approach. Practice-alone participants remained solution-oriented.

The simulations often test the doctor’s ability to ask the right questions, which stems from one’s own background knowledge in the field. But more than that, they test patience, communication skills, and empathy — the soft skills side of a profession that requires an immense amount of concrete knowledge and skill.

The findings are qualitative (classroom case studies, no control group). Students described the simulations as encouraging historical empathy, the realization that the people they study were once real human beings with normal lives. Breen concluded that the simulations worked best when integrated into a larger cycle of discussion, analysis, reflection, and research, and not as one-off engagement activities.

Participants in the ACE condition also reported higher perceived improvement in their second negotiation, a mean of 4.23 on a five-point scale. The authors built the system because negotiation skills are traditionally taught through resource-intensive seminars that most learners never get access to.

What we need are the right pedagogical mechanisms around the LLM simulation for this to really be useful. Beyond that, the “craft” of producing these virtual rooms, simulated conversations, and role-playing dialogues needs to advance and be codified across a wide range of educational contexts.
